entities.name: Huangbo Xiyun
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Huangbo Xiyun (died 855 CE) was a pivotal master in the development of Chan Buddhism during China's Tang dynasty, whose radical teachings on 'no-mind' and instantaneous enlightenment profoundly shaped the trajectory of East Asian spiritual thought. A direct dharma heir of Baizhang Huaihai and a prominent figure within the influential Hongzhou school, Huangbo's intellectual lineage traces back to Mazu Daoyi, placing him at the heart of Chan's transformation into a distinct and powerful religious movement in 9th-century China. His contributions are foundational not only to Chinese Chan but also to Japanese Zen, particularly the Rinzai school, which venerates him as a patriarch.

Residing primarily at Mount Huangbo in Fujian Province, Huangbo Xiyun's teaching methodology was characterized by direct, confrontational encounters and a profound skepticism towards scriptural study and gradual cultivation. He famously advocated for an immediate realization of one's inherent Buddha-nature, asserting that 'all the Buddhas and all sentient beings are nothing but the One Mind.' His most enduring contribution was the articulation of *wuxin* ('no-mind'), a state beyond conceptual thought and dualistic perception, which he believed was the true path to liberation. This approach, often delivered through shouts and blows, directly influenced his most famous disciple, Linji Yixuan, who would later establish the Linji school, characterized by its equally vigorous and iconoclastic style.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Huangbo Xiyun's radical teachings on 'no-mind' profoundly shaped the development of Chan Buddhism, directly inspiring the Linji school which became one of the most influential branches of Zen in East Asia. His emphasis on direct experience over scripture continues to resonate in modern Buddhist practice.
